extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of poetry, drama, music, dance, and visual arts (creative writers and critics)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for producing and judging imitative poetry and allied fine arts in the Aristotelian tradition, treating medium-specific capacities (music, dance, painting, sculpture, architecture), the role of rhythm/melody/metric form, and the aim of revealing universal form in representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art as imitation of human life and the universal form
rubrics_metrics.description: A work of art is an image of the impressions or 'phantasy pictures' made by an independent reality upon the mind of the artist; the original which it reflects is human action and character. Imitative art in its highest form (poetry) is an expression of the universal element in human life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art should eliminate transient and accidental detail to reveal the 'form' (εἶδος) or permanent, essential features of the original; the ideal exhibited is the real purified—'the ideal is the real, but rid of contradictions.' Evaluate works by how well they capture universal, essential features rather than mere particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of illusion and τὸ πιθανόν (plausible semblance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Art must be skilled in the use of illusion to give coherence and impart an air of reality; the doctrine of aesthetic semblance (τὸ πιθανόν) implies that the poet 'ought to prefer probable impossibilities to possible improbabilities.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer narrative or representational choices that achieve a convincing semblance even if they are improbably idealized; use illusion to free the aesthetic emotion from ordinary material constraints and maintain internal coherence and plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium specificity: choose the appropriate vehicle for imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Different arts reflect the image with varying directness and vividness; some imaginative subject-matter is better expressed in prose, some in verse. The essence of poetic art lies in imitation of the idea rather than in versification alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate and choose form (prose, verse, mixed metres, musical setting) by how well it serves the imitation of life/idea. Do not conflate poetic quality with mere metrical form—imitation of action/idea is the key criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm, harmony, and metre as enhancers not essentials
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhythm and harmony (and metre/melody) are causes of poetry and produce pleasure, but are regarded as 'seasoning' (ἡδύσματα) rather than the essence of poetic art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metre, melody, and rhythmic devices to enhance emotional effect and charm; judge works primarily on their imitative power and ideas, while recognizing rhythm/melody as important embellishments that intensify pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music's ethical and imitative power
rubrics_metrics.description: Music is held to be especially 'imitative'—a direct image, a copy of character. Melody even apart from words has an ethical quality; rhythms and melodies can imitate anger, mildness, courage, temperance, and their opposites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or evaluating music (or musical aspects of poetry/drama), attend to pitch, key, rhythm and scale choices as conveyors of moral/emotional character; consider music's capacity both to reflect and to shape character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of music without words and need for associations
rubrics_metrics.description: Much of music's meaning was historically derived from the associations it called up and from the emotional atmosphere around it; 'when there are no words... it is very difficult to recognise the meaning of harmony or rhythm.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To convey specific meanings through music alone, rely on established associations, contexts, or attach words; assess whether musical passages communicate intended affect or remain ambiguous without verbal anchors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Painting and sculpture render outward features and use signs/symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Painting and sculpture directly render outward and physical features and convey moral/spiritual facts largely by signs or symbols; form and colour are 'rather signs of moral qualities' and facial expression, gestures, and attitudes are natural tokens of inner life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In visual arts, employ facial expression, gesture, form, line, colour and symmetry to suggest moral/psychological qualities; recognize their comparative inferiority to music for expressing inner moral life but value natural signs for immediate suggestion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Static arts must choose a representative moment
rubrics_metrics.description: Sculpture and painting, being frozen and arrested in movement, fix eternally the feeling they portray; a single typical moment is seized and becomes representative of what precedes or follows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a single, expressive moment that will stand as emblematic of broader action or emotion; evaluate static works on how successfully that chosen instant represents the larger sequence or character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dance as an expressive art demanding knowledge and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Dancing imitates character, emotion, and action; the dancer must have genius, critical judgment of poetry, memory, mythological knowledge, and be able to reproduce legends and detail while avoiding 'terrible solecisms.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess dance on clarity/perspicuity, narrative comprehension, mastery of gestures/attitudes, and fidelity to the spirit of the subject; performers should aim to be 'understood though dumb and heard though says nothing.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural signs preferred over conventional symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Facial expressions, gestures and bodily movements are living signs taught by nature and convey meaning without a conscious inferential process; they are not merely conventional symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor natural, instinctive signs in representation to achieve immediate suggestion of inner life; reserve conventional symbolism for contexts where cultural conventions are well-understood and effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic form imposed on alien matter to free aesthetic emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: By impressing the artistic form upon a matter which is not proper to that form, art severs itself from material reality and emancipates aesthetic emotion; the union of form with alien matter produces a magical effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider imaginative combinations of form and matter that distance the work from mundane reality to evoke autonomous aesthetic emotion; evaluate how such transpositions contribute to coherence and emotional release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as the broadest imitator through language (words as symbols)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry produces effects through words (symbols) which call up images; though symbols require interpretation and vary by culture, poetry uniquely can present the widest range of human action and character and its essence is imitation of idea rather than mere metre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge poetic works by their capacity to evoke whole human situations and universal character through language; include prose mimes, dialogues, and non-metrical imitative writing under the poetic remit when they imitate life effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between imitative fine art and functional arts (architecture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture was classed among the useful arts by the Greeks because it lacked the 'imitative' quality essential to fine art; decorative sculpture on buildings may be imitative but the building-as-whole is not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying or evaluating works, distinguish functional/utility-driven constructions from imitative fine art; evaluate decorative or sculptural elements on their imitative merits but not the functional structure as fine art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compositional choices (melody vs harmony) affect expressivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Music that treats the voice as one instrument among many (harmony-based) tends to curtail the voice's dramatic and emotional effect; ancient melodic/rhythmic systems preserved subtle vocal inflexions akin to speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a compositional approach aligned with desired expressive aims: privileging melody and vocal inflection for direct dramatic/emotional expression, or harmony for independent musical creation; evaluate musical textures accordingly.
